content: James fibers, also referred to as atrioventricular bypass fibers, are specialized fibers that connect the atrial fibers to the bundle of His by penetrating through the atrioventricular (AV) node. These fibers bypass the normal conduction system of the heart. Accessory bypass fibers that connect the atrial fibers to the bundle of His via the AV node were first described by James in 1961. James fibers originate in the lower atrium and terminate in the lower AV node. They connect the atrial fibers above with the bundle of His below. As they penetrate the AV node, these fibers travel along the posterior internodal tract, running alongside other fibers, but they make contact with the AV node at a more distal point compared to other posterior input fibers. Since they do not completely bypass the AV node and are found in all hearts, James suggested that these fibers may not truly be accessory fibers as previously assumed. Unlike the AV node, James fibers lack rate-slowing properties and are capable of conducting electrical impulses at a significantly higher rate. This rapid conduction can result in inadequate ventricular filling and emptying, leading to hemodynamic instability. If not corrected promptly, this can progress to ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death. Conduction through James fibers is one of the potential mechanisms for a short PR interval observed in Lown-Ganong-Levine (LGL) syndrome. Because these fibers pass through the normal conduction system, the QRS complex following the short PR interval in LGL syndrome is typically normal. This distinguishes it from Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, where the QRS complex is wide and abnormal in appearance. In rare cases where medical therapy fails to manage LGL syndrome, radiofrequency ablation of the AV node and its accessory fibers may be considered as a treatment option.
